Learning objective: To be able to review outsourcing needs.
 1 1.1  Insurance aspects
One important factor with outsourcing, is that while it may be possible to outsource a number of activities, the 
regulatory requirements cannot usually be delegated, and the insurance company remains liable to the regulatory

authority for performance.
Outsourcing has had mixed reviews and there are examples where it can work well – for example outsourcing 
medical claims to providers with a good track record, and other examples where lack of a proven track record and 
total underestimation of the work involved has led to disaster.
Certain Lloyd’s syndicates have outsourced motor claims successfully – a typical situation whereby smaller or -

ganisations can group their needs together and reach economies of scale and a much better result for the insured.
The vast majority of US firms use outsourcing in one form or another, whether it be human resources, or payroll, 
or accounting or distribution, and it is likely it will be a form of organisation more prevalent in the future. Even using 
the resources of reinsurers to quote more complex risks, or to introduce or expand certain lines of business could

be seen as a form of outsourcing.
The distribution of insurance products via a broker is also a form of outsourcing marketing and production.
The issue with claims is that, more than any other activity, poor claims handling can quickly tarnish the reputation 
of the insurance company and create serious issues with the regulator, and for this reason very special care needs 
to be taken when considering outsourcing in this area.

to be taken when considering outsourcing in this area.
However it is worth remembering that, depending on the amount of reinsurance purchased, a lot of an insurance 
company’s ability to pay a claim rests on the timely performance of its reinsurers, thus, like it or not, many insurance 
companies are already relying considerably on the performance of organisations outside of their direct control.

Essentially an insurance company is made up of capital, risk expertise, and licences to write business. With a 
number of investors looking to expand their portfolios, there is also the prospect of insurance companies offering 
outsourcing services to entrepreneurs who are looking for risk expertise and licences to write business. Fronting is 
already a form of outsourcing where insurance companies offer the licences they have to write business to captives

who need those licences to cover business in territories where they themselves have no licence.
Outsourcing can be a two way business.
 1 1.2 Reinsurance aspects
With the new wave of insurance linked securities and hedge funds offering a variety of capacities, outsourcing has 
certainly become a two-way business for reinsurers.
A number of reinsurers have offered their underwriting services to hedge funds and licences to issue paper on

behalf of  hedge funds, and this has been a win-win situation for both parties.
Given the savings that can result in overhead costs from such an arrangement, there will likely be pressure on 
traditional reinsurance companies to review their form of organisation.

This course has been designed to expand the knowledge base built in earlier courses and especially to enhance 
your understanding of claims management. The ability to correctly negotiate and adjust claims, to pay only those

that fall within the cover, and to pay the right amount, all the time providing the claimant with a polite and efficient 
service is at the very core of what a (re)insurance company is all about.
Equally important is to follow the claim through the company and into any reinsurance or retrocession programme 
and to be sure all recoveries from those covers have been made and received.

and to be sure all recoveries from those covers have been made and received.
It is also very important that the right processes are in place to alert management to any claim trends, so that im -
mediate corrective action can be taken, and equally that any complaints are promptly dealt with.
Where dealing with consumers, the claims service and fair treatment of clients are at the very heart of regulation,

because at the end of the day, this is what our business is about: assuring security of mind by paying claims in the 
event of an insured loss.

1.1 I NTRODUCTION  
1.1.1 This chapter provides guidanc e on sound practices in carrying out 
insurance business and covers the core  activities of product development, 
pricing, underwriting, claims handli ng and reinsurance management.  It 
articulates broad principles that should be embedded in a risk management

contained in this chapter are applic able for both life and general insurance 
business, unless explicitly stated otherwise.

guidelines issued or to be issued by t he MAS, in particular “Guidelines on

1.2 F UNDAMENTALS  
1.2.1 Product development, pricing, underwriting, claims handling and 
reinsurance management repr esent the core activities of an insurer.  In 
carrying out these core activities, an insurer will face a wide range of risks 
which are often interlinked and if not  properly managed, could threaten the

which are often interlinked and if not  properly managed, could threaten the 
ability of the institution to achieve its objectives and sustain it s viability.  An 
insurer should therefore adopt a holis tic approach to adequately identify, 
measure, control and m onitor these risks.

  6 
 
 
1 BOARD AND SENIOR MANAGEMENT  RESPONSIBILITIES  
 
1.1 MAS expects  the Board and senior management of financial institutions 
to set the right tone in conducting marketing and distribution activities to customers 
in a responsible and professional manner .  MAS  will also hold the Board and senior 
management  accountable for ensuring that t heir financial institution’s  business

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
management  accountable for ensuring that t heir financial institution’s  business 
conduct practices are in line with the objectives of the Guidelines.  
 
1.2 The Board and senior management should ensure that the safeguards 
elaborated in section 2 are incorporated into  the financial institution’s policies, 
systems and processes relating to its marketing and distribution activities, as 
relevant .  They should  also ensure that  the risks posed by their  financial

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
relevant .  They should  also ensure that  the risks posed by their  financial 
institution’s  marketing and distribution activities  are properly assessed and 
addressed .  Where issues arise that may compromise the interests of customers , 
the financial institution should consider instituting measures that are more stringent 
than those  set out in the Guidelines.

2 MARKET CONDUCT SAFEGUARDS  
 
2.1 Exercising  adequate oversight of marketing and distribution 
activities  
 
2.1.1  Marketing and distribution activities at retailers and public places increase 
the reach of financial institutions to members of the public.  If such activities are 
not properly managed,  they could lead to heightened market conduct risks to

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
not properly managed,  they could lead to heightened market conduct risks to 
customers .  To mitigate the se risks, financial institutions should maintain adequate 
oversight of their marketing and distribution arrangements at these  places to 
ensure that their representatives enga ge in proper marketing, sales and advisory 
practices.  
 
2.1.2  Financial institutions should carefully assess the potential market conduct

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
practices.  
 
2.1.2  Financial institutions should carefully assess the potential market conduct 
risks that could arise and ensure that they devote sufficient resources to, and put 
in place sound processes for, the oversight of their marketing and distribution  
arrangements at retailers and public places.  These are elaborated in Safeguards  
1 to 4.  
 
Safeguard 1  
 
2.1.3  Marketing and distribution arrangements  are usually held at public areas

2.1.3  Marketing and distribution arrangements  are usually held at public areas 
or at the premises of retailers with high foot traffic  (e.g. roadshows at shopping 
malls or supermarket chains) .  Some customers may find it difficult to make a

free-look or cooling -off period, to ensure that customers have understood

Financial institutions are expected to implement this  safegu ard for the sale

considered decision in such circumstances and could make impulse purchases

customers when it s representatives  prospect and close sales at retailers and public 
places to ensure th ese customers  are fully aware of the features and risks of the

places to ensure th ese customers  are fully aware of the features and risks of the

free-look or cooling off period (referred to as “specified period”) and should be

2.1.6  The call -backs may be conducted by a supervisor of the representative

2.1.7  The financial institution may choose to survey customers using  other

2.1.8  The financ ial institution should also have procedures to effectively

customer base.  
 
2.1.8  The financ ial institution should also have procedures to effectively

Safeguard 2  
 
Financial institutions should conduct regular mystery shopping and site 
visits to monitor and ensure that the marketing, sales and advisory 
practices of representatives at retailers and public places are conducted 
in line with  their  internal standards and procedures as well as the  
Guidelines on Standards of C onduct for Marketing and Distribution

Financial i nstitution s are not required to implement this safeguard for the 
sale of banking and general insurance products and services , where the 
banking or general insurance  product or service purchased is related to 
the product or service that the customer has bought3. 
 
2.1.9  Customers often rely on the representatives of financial institutions to

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
2.1.9  Customers often rely on the representatives of financial institutions to 
explain to them the features, risks, and fees and charges of financial products and 
services, and recommend financial products and services that are suitable for them.  
As the purchase of financial products  or services may require long -term and/or 
significant financial commitment by customers , it is important that customers are

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
significant financial commitment by customers , it is important that customers are 
treated fairly and are recommended  financial products  or services that meet their 
needs . 
 
2.1.10  However, some representatives may be motivated by the commissions, 
incentives, and other rewards that are tied to their sales performance and engage 
in inappropriate practices such as product pushing and misrepresentation, in order

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
in inappropriate practices such as product pushing and misrepresentation, in order 
to meet sales targets.  As such, financial institutions should institute regular checks 
on their representatives’ marketing, sales and advisory activities.    
 
2.1.11  Financ ial institution s should generally conduct both mystery shopping 
exercises and site visits as they complement each other in a financial institution’s

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
exercises and site visits as they complement each other in a financial institution’s 
oversight of its marketing and distribution activities  at retailers and public places . 
Mystery shopping exe rcises entail  more rigorous checks on representatives’ sales 
and advisory practices, while site visits ensure that marketing and distribution 
activities are conducted professionally in an ongoing manner  as they can be 
conducted more frequently . However, t he financial institution may choose to

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

conducted more frequently . However, t he financial institution may choose to

conduct mystery shopping in place of site visits as long as it ensures that there are

2.1.12  The financial institution should ensure that its mystery shopping exercise s 
and site visits provide sufficient coverage of its marketing and distribution 
arrangements, taking into account the scale of its business and marketing and

Safeguard 3  
 
Financial institutions should separately track and monitor complaints

Safeguard 3  
 
Financial institutions should separately track and monitor complaints 
arising from their marketing, sales and advisory activities at retailers and 
public places.  Complaints statistics should also be reported to senior 
management on a regular basis.  
 
2.1.13  Comp laints can be an important indicator of potential problems occurring 
as a result of  a financial institution’s business activities. The monitoring of

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
as a result of  a financial institution’s business activities. The monitoring of 
complaints allows financial institutions to identify issues arising from their 
marketing and distribution a ctivities and implement timely measures to address 
these issues.  
 
2.1.14   Currently, financial institutions have in place their own complaints 
monitoring mechanisms and resolution frameworks to track  and resolve complaints

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
monitoring mechanisms and resolution frameworks to track  and resolve complaints 
on their  business conduct practices, service standards and commercial practices. 
Financial institution s should enhance their existing complaints monitoring 
mechanism s to separately track complaints arising from their marketing and 
distribution arrangements.  Where  a financial institution receives a large number 
of complaints relating to such arrangements , it should take steps to identify the

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
of complaints relating to such arrangements , it should take steps to identify the 
root cause of the problem and implement measures to rectify the issue promptly 
and effectively.  This should also apply when there are complaints relating to 
marketing and distribution activities at a specific location, by a specific 
representative or group of representatives, for specific financial products , or with  
customers of a certain profile.

2.1.15  The results of the complaint s monitoring and  analysis done on the 
complaints statistics should be reported to senior management on a regular basis.

Financial institution s should maintain a register containing information on 
their marketing and distribution arrangements  at retailers and public 
places.

their marketing and distribution arrangements  at retailers and public 
places.  
 
2.1.16  When financial institutions  conduct marketing and distribution activities, 
their representatives may be deployed to various  locations  and there may be 
concurrent events  happening at the same time.   In order to exercise effective 
oversight of their marketing, sales and advisory activities at retailers and public 
places, financial institutions should maintain proper records of their marketing and

places, financial institutions should maintain proper records of their marketing and 
distribution arrangements.  This w ill also allow financia l institutions to more easily 
identify the source, nature and cause of any issue or complaint.  
 
2.1.17  Financial institution s should maintain a register containing information on 
their marketing and distribution arrangements at retailers and public places.  The 
register should minimally  keep records of:

register should minimally  keep records of:  
 
(a) the locations  of the financial institution’s marketin g and distribution

(b) the period and dur ation of the arrangements and/or events;  
(c) the identities of representatives and supervisors involved; and  
(d) the financial products  and/or services marketed or distributed.  
 
2.1.18  The financial institution should consider maintaining records of other

if they are deem ed necessary for better  oversight of its marketing and distribution

2.2 Conducting  marketing , sales and advisory activities in a 
professional manner  
 
2.2.1  Representatives who market and sell financial products  and services on

2.2.1  Representatives who market and sell financial products  and services on 
behalf of their financial institutions should be competent , adopt ethical practices  
and uphold the professional image of the financial industry.  Financial institutions

currently  have in place internal codes of professional conduct  and requirements

that they are intended to achieve .  In addition, financial institutions should put in

Safeguard 5 
 
Financial institution s and their representatives should conduct 
themselves in a professional manner at all times when prospecting for and 
dealing with customers at retailers and public places.  They must not cause 
annoyance by being unreasonably persistent or by placing undue

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
annoyance by being unreasonably persistent or by placing undue 
pressure on members of the public to purchase any financial product or 
service.  
 
2.2.3  The m arketing and distribution activities conducted by financial 
institutions  at public areas or at the premises of retailers  increase the ir visibility and 
widen their reach to a larger group of potential customers.   It is therefore important 
that representatives conduct themselves professional ly when prospecting for and

metadata.source: d:\ComplianceIQ\data\regulatory\mas\MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf
metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
that representatives conduct themselves professional ly when prospecting for and 
dealing with customers at retailers and public places.    
 
2.2.4  The financial institution  should incorporate i nto its policies and 
procedures  the standards of  professional conduct that it expects  of its 
representatives.  Appropriate actions should be taken against representatives who 
engage in  unethical or unprofessional conduct  when prospecting for customers at

metadata.file_name: MAS Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities.pdf

text:
engage in  unethical or unprofessional conduct  when prospecting for customers at 
retailers and public places.  Examples of inappropriate and unprofessional conduct 
include being rude , unreasona ble and aggressive, or causing annoyance by being 
overly persistent or  by placing undue pressure on member s of the public to 
purchase financial products  or services .

Safeguard 6 
 
Financial institution s should ensure that their representatives clearly 
disclose upf ront their identities and the financial institution  they represent

Where financial institution s market third -party products  or services , they 
should ensure that their representatives disclose and explain to customers

as such encounters are usually not anticipated by  customer s as they would not

product  or service .

institution should ensure that its  representatives clearly disclose and explain to

institution should ensure that its  representatives clearly disclose and explain to

premises, the financial institution should ensure that  its representati ves clearly 
disclose to customers the tie-up between the financial institution and the retailer, 
and explain each party’s roles and responsibilities.  In this regard, t he financial

awareness of their respective brands and range of products and services offered.

awareness of their respective brands and range of products and services offered.  
The financial institution should ensure  that any  co-branding efforts with retailers

are not mis leading and do not create any confusion among customers . The

1. Definitions
1.1 Cyber Incident:

A Cyber Incident is defined as any event or series of events, whether accidental, negligent, or intentional, that lead to unauthorized access, use, disclosure, modification, or destruction of the Policyholder’s computer systems or data. This includes, but is not limited to, incidents involving hacking, malware, ransomware, phishing, denial of service attacks, social engineering tactics, and insider threats
. Cyber Incidents are further categorized into minor, moderate, and severe based on the impact and extent of damage.
1.2 Data Breach:

Data Breach refers to the unauthorized acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of confidential, sensitive, or personal data that compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of such data. This definition encompasses breaches involving electronic data as well as physical records, and includes data held by third-party service providers

. The breach is considered significant if it involves personally identifiable information (PII), payment card information (PCI), or other sensitive data regulated under applicable data protection laws.
1.3 Business Interruption Loss:

Business Interruption Loss is the loss of net income that the Policyholder sustains due to the necessary suspension of business operations resulting directly from a Cyber Incident. This includes losses incurred during the period of restoration, which is the time required to restore normal business operations, and any additional expenses incurred to minimize the suspension of business
. The calculation of loss considers historical revenue, growth trends, and seasonal variations, and includes costs associated with alternative solutions and temporary setups.

1.4 Policy Limit:
The Policy Limit is the maximum amount payable under this contract for all covered losses occurring during the policy period. This limit applies regardless of the number of claims made or the number of insured parties under the policy. The Policy Limit encompasses all coverage sections, including legal liabilities, data breach costs, and other specific coverages outlined in the policy.

1.5 Deductible:
The Deductible is the amount the Policyholder is required to pay out-of-pocket for each claim before the insurance coverage becomes applicable. The deductible applies separately to each incident or claim and is intended to ensure that the Policyholder maintains a reasonable level of risk management and prevention. The deductible amount may be adjusted based on the risk profile and cybersecurity maturity of the Policyholder.

1.6 Third-Party Claim:
A Third-Party Claim is any claim made by an external party against the Policyholder as a result of a Cyber Incident. This includes claims for damages, legal fees, and other costs associated with the incident. Third-party claims can arise from customers, partners, vendors, or regulatory bodies and may involve allegations of negligence, breach of contract, or failure to comply with data protection laws.

1.7 Insured Party:
The Insured Party refers to Tech Solutions Ltd. and any additional insured entities or individuals explicitly named in the policy endorsements. This includes subsidiaries, affiliates, and joint ventures, provided they are engaged in similar business activities and adhere to the same risk management practices as the primary Policyholder.

1.8 Malware:
Malware refers to malicious software designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems. This includes viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, adware, and ransomware. Coverage for malware-related incidents includes both direct damages and associated costs of eradication and system restoration.

1.9 Phishing:
Phishing is a social engineering attack where attackers impersonate legitimate entities to trick individuals into providing sensitive information such as login credentials or financial data. Phishing can occur via email, phone, or other communication channels. The policy covers losses arising from successful phishing attacks that lead to unauthorized access or data breaches.

1.10 Social Engineering Fraud:
Social Engineering Fraud involves manipulation tactics used by attackers to deceive individuals into divulging confidential information or performing actions that compromise security. This includes pretexting, baiting, and other forms of deception. Coverage for social engineering fraud extends to financial losses and costs of education and training to prevent future occurrences.
2. Coverage
2.1 Network Security Liability:

This coverage provides protection against legal liability arising from a Third-Party Claim due to a Cyber Incident affecting the Policyholder’s computer systems. Covered incidents include unauthorized access, transmission of malicious code, and denial of service attacks. Legal defense costs, settlement amounts, and damages awarded to third parties are included in the coverage
. The policy also extends coverage to liabilities arising from failure to prevent unauthorized access to third-party systems through the Policyholder's network.
2.2 Data Breach Costs:

Data Breach Costs cover expenses incurred by the Policyholder in response to a Data Breach. Covered expenses include, but are not limited to, costs associated with notifying affected individuals, providing credit monitoring services, engaging public relations consultants to mitigate reputational damage, and hiring forensic investigators to determine the scope and cause of the breach. The policy also covers legal fees for navigating data protection regulations and potential class action lawsuits
2.3 Business Interruption:

Coverage for Business Interruption includes loss of income and additional expenses incurred due to a Cyber Incident that disrupts normal business operations. This coverage is subject to a waiting period of 12 hours, after which the loss of income will be calculated based on the Policyholder’s historical financial records. Additional expenses may include costs incurred to expedite the restoration of business operations, such as hiring temporary staff or leasing replacement equipment
. The policy also provides coverage for contingent business interruption, which applies when a Cyber Incident affects a critical supplier or service provider.
2.4 Cyber Extortion:

Cyber Extortion coverage applies to payments made to prevent or terminate a cyber extortion threat, such as a ransomware demand. Coverage is contingent upon the Policyholder obtaining prior written approval from SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. before making any extortion payments. The policy also covers costs associated with hiring cybersecurity experts to negotiate with extortionists and restore data
. Additionally, the policy provides coverage for loss of funds transferred to cybercriminals as a result of a covered cyber extortion incident.

2.5 Regulatory Defense and Penalties:
This coverage provides for legal expenses and fines incurred due to regulatory investigations or proceedings following a Cyber Incident. Coverage is subject to the applicability of local laws and includes costs for legal representation, fines imposed by regulatory bodies, and compliance audits required by regulators. The policy also covers costs associated with implementing corrective actions mandated by regulatory authorities to prevent future incidents.
2.6 Crisis Management and Public Relations:

In the event of a Cyber Incident, this coverage provides access to crisis management and public relations services to manage the impact on the Policyholder’s reputation. Services include media communication strategies, stakeholder engagement, and ongoing public relations support to rebuild trust with clients and partners. The policy also covers the costs of conducting customer satisfaction surveys and brand reputation analysis to assess the impact of the incident and guide recovery efforts.
2.7 Technology Errors and Omissions Liability:

This coverage applies to claims arising from errors, omissions, or negligent acts in the provision of technology services or products by the Policyholder. Examples include software malfunctions, coding errors, or failures to meet service level agreements. Coverage includes legal defense costs, settlements, and damages awarded to third parties. This section of the policy is particularly relevant for Policyholders engaged in software development, IT consulting, or managed services.

2.8 Media Liability:
Media Liability coverage applies to claims arising from the Policyholder’s media activities, including content dissemination through websites, social media, and other online platforms. Covered claims include allegations of copyright infringement, defamation, invasion of privacy, and emotional distress caused by published content. Coverage includes legal defense costs, settlements, and damages awarded to third parties.

2.9 Reputation Repair Costs:
This coverage provides reimbursement for costs incurred to repair the Policyholder’s reputation following a Cyber Incident. Covered expenses include hiring public relations firms, conducting rebranding campaigns, and engaging media consultants to manage public perception. The policy also covers costs associated with conducting market research to assess the impact on brand reputation and customer loyalty.

2.10 Telecommunications Fraud:
Coverage for Telecommunications Fraud applies to losses resulting from unauthorized use of the Policyholder’s telecommunications systems, such as PBX hacking or toll fraud. The policy covers the cost of unauthorized calls, system audits, and implementation of enhanced security measures to prevent future incidents.
3. Exclusions

3.1 Prior Cyber Incidents:
This policy excludes coverage for any Cyber Incidents that occurred prior to the policy inception date, regardless of when the incident is discovered or reported. This exclusion also applies to any claims arising from incidents that were known to the Policyholder before the policy start date. The Policyholder is required to disclose any known incidents or vulnerabilities during the underwriting process, and failure to do so may result in denial of coverage.

3.2 Intentional Acts:
Coverage is excluded for any fraudulent, dishonest, or criminal acts committed by the Policyholder or its employees. This includes acts intentionally committed to cause harm or obtain unauthorized benefit, as well as any collusion or conspiracy to commit such acts. The policy also excludes coverage for acts committed with reckless disregard for the consequences, where the Policyholder could have reasonably foreseen the potential for harm.

3.3 War and Terrorism:
Losses resulting from acts of war, whether declared or undeclared, or acts of terrorism are not covered under this policy. This exclusion applies to both cyber and physical acts of war or terrorism that result in a Cyber Incident. The policy does not cover losses arising from government-imposed sanctions, embargoes, or acts of rebellion.

3.4 Bodily Injury or Property Damage:
This policy does not cover claims for bodily injury to persons or physical damage to tangible property. Coverage is strictly limited to losses involving electronic data and systems. The policy excludes any claims arising from injury or death of individuals, damage to real estate, or physical assets such as equipment or infrastructure.

3.5 Patent Infringement:
Claims arising out of the infringement of patents, trade secrets, or intellectual property rights are excluded from coverage. This exclusion applies to both intentional and unintentional acts of infringement. The policyholder is advised to secure separate intellectual property insurance to address such risks.

3.6 Contractual Liabilities:
This policy excludes coverage for liabilities assumed by the Policyholder under any contract or agreement, unless such liability would have existed in the absence of the contract or agreement. The exclusion applies to indemnity clauses, warranties, and service level agreements that extend beyond the Policyholder’s standard business operations.

3.7 Fines and Penalties (Not Covered by Regulatory Defense):
Fines and penalties imposed by regulatory bodies that are not covered under the Regulatory Defense and Penalties section are excluded. This includes punitive or exemplary damages intended to punish or deter wrongdoing. Coverage does not extend to fines arising from willful non-compliance with regulatory requirements or intentional violations of law.

3.8 Infrastructure Failures:
This policy does not cover losses resulting from failures of critical infrastructure such as power grids, telecommunications networks, or internet service providers, unless directly caused by a Cyber Incident affecting the Policyholder’s systems. The Policyholder is responsible for implementing redundancy and backup measures to mitigate the impact of infrastructure failures.

3.9 Loss of Market Share:
Claims for loss of market share, competitive disadvantage, or loss of goodwill resulting from a Cyber Incident are excluded from coverage. The policy focuses on tangible financial losses and direct costs associated with the incident, and does not extend to speculative or indirect economic impacts.

3.10 Unreported Incidents:
Coverage is excluded for any Cyber Incidents that are not reported to SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. within the specified notification period. Timely reporting is essential for effective claim processing and mitigation efforts, and failure to comply with reporting requirements may result in denial of coverage.
4. Claims Process

4.1 Notice of Claim:
The Policyholder must provide written notice to SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. within 48 hours of discovering a Cyber Incident that may give rise to a claim under this policy. The notice should include a description of the incident, date and time of occurrence, and any immediate actions taken to mitigate the impact. The Policyholder should utilize the designated claims portal or contact the claims hotline for prompt assistance.

4.2 Documentation:
The Policyholder is required to submit all relevant documentation and information related to the claim, including but not limited to incident reports, financial records, forensic investigation results, and correspondence with third parties. The documentation should provide a comprehensive overview of the incident, impact assessment, and recovery efforts. Failure to provide complete and accurate documentation may result in denial of the claim.

4.3 Cooperation:
The Policyholder must fully cooperate with SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. in the investigation and defense of any claim. This includes providing access to systems, records, and personnel as necessary to assess the extent of the Cyber Incident and determine coverage eligibility. Cooperation also involves participating in interviews, providing sworn statements, and assisting in the recovery of losses through subrogation efforts.

4.4 Settlement:
SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. retains the right to settle any claim at its discretion. The Policyholder shall not admit liability, make any payment, or agree to any settlement without the prior written consent of SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. Any settlement made without such consent may result in denial of coverage for that claim. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. will consider the Policyholder’s input and business interests in any settlement negotiations.

4.5 Subrogation Rights:
Upon payment of a claim, SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. is subrogated to all rights of the Policyholder to recover from any third party responsible for the loss. The Policyholder agrees to execute any documents and take any actions necessary to secure these rights. Subrogation efforts may include pursuing recovery from vendors, service providers, or other parties whose actions contributed to the Cyber Incident.

4.6 Expert Consultation:
SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. may engage independent experts, such as cybersecurity consultants, legal advisors, or forensic investigators, to assist in the evaluation and resolution of claims. The Policyholder agrees to cooperate with these experts and provide access to relevant information and systems. Costs associated with expert consultation are covered under the policy, subject to prior approval by SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd.

4.7 Claim Dispute Resolution:
In the event of a dispute regarding the coverage or settlement of a claim, the parties agree to engage in mediation as a preliminary step before pursuing formal legal action. Mediation shall be conducted by a neutral third party, with costs shared equally by both parties. If mediation fails to resolve the dispute, the parties may proceed to arbitration or litigation, as specified in the policy conditions.
5. Policy Conditions

5.1 Confidentiality:
The terms and conditions of this policy, including any endorsements and amendments, must be kept confidential by both parties. Disclosure of policy details to any third party is prohibited without the prior written consent of the other party, except as required by law or regulatory authority. Breach of confidentiality may result in termination of coverage and potential legal action.

5.2 Subrogation:
SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. reserves the right to recover any payment made under this policy from third parties responsible for the loss. The Policyholder agrees to assign all rights to pursue recovery to SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. and to assist in any recovery efforts. The Policyholder is prohibited from waiving subrogation rights without the written consent of SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd.
5.3 Policy Cancellation:

Either party may cancel this policy with 30 days' written notice to the other party. In the event of cancellation, SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. will refund the unearned premium on a pro-rata basis, provided no claims have been made during the policy period. If a claim has been made, the premium is considered fully earned and non-refundable. The Policyholder may cancel the policy immediately if SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. fails to fulfill its obligations under the policy.

5.4 Jurisdiction:
This policy shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of India. Any disputes arising under or in connection with this policy shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of New Delhi, India. The parties agree to submit to the jurisdiction of these courts and waive any objections based on venue or forum non-conveniens.

5.5 Inspections and Audits:
SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. reserves the right to conduct inspections and audits of the Policyholder’s premises, systems, and records to verify compliance with policy terms and assess risk exposure. The Policyholder agrees to provide reasonable access and cooperation during such inspections. Audits may include assessments of cybersecurity practices, incident response plans, and compliance with regulatory requirements.
5.6 Risk Mitigation:

The Policyholder agrees to implement and maintain appropriate cybersecurity measures and controls to mitigate the risk of Cyber Incidents. This includes, but is not limited to, regular system updates, employee training, and incident response planning. Failure to maintain adequate security measures may affect coverage eligibility. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. may provide recommendations for risk mitigation practices, and compliance with these recommendations may be a condition of coverage.

5.7 Changes in Risk Profile:
The Policyholder must notify SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. of any material changes in its risk profile, such as mergers, acquisitions, changes in business operations, or significant upgrades to IT infrastructure. Failure to disclose material changes may result in denial of coverage for claims arising from the undisclosed changes. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. reserves the right to adjust premiums or policy terms based on changes in risk exposure.

5.8 Legal Compliance:
The Policyholder must comply with all applicable laws, regulations, and industry standards related to cybersecurity and data protection. Non-compliance may affect coverage eligibility and result in denial of claims arising from regulatory violations. The Policyholder is encouraged to seek legal counsel to ensure compliance with evolving legal requirements.
6. General Provisions

6.1 Entire Agreement:
This contract constitutes the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior negotiations, representations, and agreements. No oral or written statements made by either party prior to the execution of this policy shall be considered part of the agreement. The Policyholder acknowledges that no representations or warranties have been made other than those expressly set forth in this policy.

6.2 Amendments:
Any amendments or modifications to this policy must be in writing and signed by both parties. No waiver of any provision of this policy shall be effective unless made in writing and signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought. Amendments may include changes to coverage limits, deductibles, endorsements, or other policy terms.

6.3 Notification:
All notices required under this policy must be in writing and delivered to the respective party's address as stated in this contract. Notices may be delivered by hand, courier, registered post, or electronic mail with confirmation of receipt. The Policyholder must promptly update contact information to ensure receipt of important communications.

6.4 Severability:
If any provision of this policy is found to be invalid or unenforceable, the remaining provisions shall remain in full force and effect. The parties agree to negotiate in good faith to replace any invalid or unenforceable provision with a valid and enforceable provision that achieves the intended purpose. The invalidity of any provision shall not affect the validity of the entire policy.

6.5 No Waiver:
The failure of either party to enforce any right or provision of this policy shall not constitute a waiver of such right or provision. A waiver of any provision of this policy shall not be deemed a waiver of any other provision, nor shall it affect the enforceability of that provision in any other instance. The rights and remedies provided in this policy are cumulative and not exclusive of any other rights or remedies available under law.

6.6 Force Majeure:
Neither party shall be liable for any failure or delay in performance under this policy due to causes beyond their reasonable control, including acts of God, natural disasters, acts of war or terrorism, civil disturbances, and government actions. In the event of a force majeure, the affected party shall promptly notify the other party and make reasonable efforts to resume performance as soon as practicable.

6.7 Assignment:
The Policyholder shall not assign or transfer any rights or obligations under this policy without the prior written consent of SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. Any attempted assignment without such consent shall be void. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. may assign its rights and obligations under this policy to a successor entity in the event of a merger, acquisition, or corporate restructuring.
7. Endorsements

7.1 Additional Insured Endorsement:
This endorsement includes additional insured parties as specified in the schedule attached to this policy. The additional insured parties are entitled to the same coverage as the primary Policyholder, subject to the terms and conditions of the policy. The endorsement may include joint ventures, subsidiaries, or other affiliated entities engaged in similar business activities.

7.2 Increased Coverage Limit Endorsement:
This endorsement increases the coverage limit to INR 15,000,000 for an additional premium of INR 150,000. The increased limit applies to all covered losses occurring during the policy period, subject to the same terms and conditions as the original policy. The Policyholder may request further increases in coverage limits based on demonstrated risk exposure and compliance with risk mitigation practices.

7.3 Extended Reporting Period Endorsement:
This endorsement provides for an extended reporting period of 12 months following the expiration or termination of the policy. During this period, the Policyholder may report claims arising from Cyber Incidents that occurred during the original policy period. The extended reporting period is subject to the payment of an additional premium and is intended to provide continuity of coverage for incidents that may not be immediately discovered.

7.4 Technology Services Endorsement:
This endorsement extends coverage to include liabilities arising from the provision of technology services by the Policyholder. Covered services include software development, IT consulting, and managed security services, subject to the terms and conditions of the policy. The endorsement also covers liabilities arising from the failure to meet service level agreements or contractual obligations related to technology services.
7.5 Social Engineering Fraud Endorsement:

This endorsement provides coverage for financial losses resulting from social engineering fraud, including phishing and pretexting attacks. Coverage includes reimbursement for funds transferred to cybercriminals as a result of fraudulent instructions and costs associated with implementing enhanced security measures to prevent future occurrences. The endorsement requires the Policyholder to implement specific controls, such as dual authorization for fund transfers, to qualify for coverage.

7.6 Cloud Services Endorsement:
This endorsement extends coverage to Cyber Incidents involving the use of cloud services, including data breaches, service disruptions, and unauthorized access to data stored in cloud environments. The Policyholder is required to ensure that cloud service providers adhere to industry-standard security practices and provide regular security audits. Coverage includes costs associated with restoring data and mitigating the impact of cloud service disruptions.
8. Risk Management Guidelines

8.1 Cybersecurity Framework:
The Policyholder is encouraged to adopt a recognized cybersecurity framework, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework or ISO/IEC 27001, to guide risk management practices. The framework should address key areas such as risk assessment, access control, incident response, and continuous monitoring. Compliance with the chosen framework may be a condition of coverage.

8.2 Employee Training:
The Policyholder must implement regular cybersecurity awareness training for all employees, contractors, and third-party partners. Training should cover topics such as phishing detection, password management, and safe browsing practices. The Policyholder should maintain records of training completion and update training materials to address emerging threats.

8.3 Access Control and Authentication:
The Policyholder is required to implement robust access control measures, including multi-factor authentication, least privilege access, and regular review of user access rights. Access to sensitive data and systems should be restricted to authorized personnel only, and all access should be logged and monitored for suspicious activity.

8.4 Incident Response Planning:
The Policyholder must develop and maintain an incident response plan that outlines procedures for identifying, responding to, and recovering from Cyber Incidents. The plan should include roles and responsibilities, communication protocols, and escalation procedures. Regular testing and updates of the incident response plan are essential to ensure its effectiveness.

8.5 Data Encryption and Protection:
The Policyholder is required to implement data encryption for sensitive data at rest and in transit. Additional data protection measures, such as data loss prevention (DLP) tools and regular data backups, should be in place to prevent unauthorized access and data breaches. The Policyholder should conduct regular vulnerability assessments to identify and address potential security gaps.

8.6 Third-Party Risk Management:
The Policyholder must assess and manage risks associated with third-party vendors and service providers. This includes conducting due diligence, establishing security requirements in contracts, and monitoring compliance with security standards. The Policyholder should require third parties to report any Cyber Incidents that may impact the Policyholder’s systems or data.

8.7 Regular Security Audits:
The Policyholder is encouraged to conduct regular security audits and penetration testing to identify vulnerabilities and assess the effectiveness of security controls. Audits should be performed by qualified cybersecurity professionals and include recommendations for remediation. The Policyholder should address identified vulnerabilities in a timely manner and document corrective actions taken.

8.8 Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery:
The Policyholder must maintain a business continuity and disaster recovery plan to ensure the resumption of critical business operations in the event of a Cyber Incident. The plan should include contingency measures, such as alternative communication channels and backup systems, and be regularly tested and updated. The Policyholder should conduct post-incident reviews to evaluate the effectiveness of the plan and identify areas for improvement.
9. Case Studies and Hypothetical Scenarios
9.1 Case Study 1: Ransomware Attack on Financial Systems

In this scenario, Tech Solutions Ltd. experiences a ransomware attack that encrypts critical financial data, rendering accounting systems inoperable. The Policyholder quickly engages cybersecurity experts to contain the spread of the malware and begins negotiations with the attackers for decryption keys. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. approves the payment of a ransom demand under the Cyber Extortion coverage, and the Policyholder successfully regains access to its data
. The Policyholder also utilizes Business Interruption coverage to recover lost income during the downtime and implements enhanced security measures to prevent future incidents.
9.2 Case Study 2: Data Breach of Customer Records

Following a sophisticated phishing attack, Tech Solutions Ltd. discovers a data breach involving the unauthorized access of customer records, including personally identifiable information (PII). The Policyholder immediately notifies affected individuals and offers credit monitoring services, as required by data protection regulations. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. covers the costs of notification, credit monitoring, and public relations efforts to manage the reputational impact
. The Policyholder also benefits from Regulatory Defense and Penalties coverage to navigate regulatory investigations and potential fines.
9.3 Case Study 3: Denial of Service Attack on E-Commerce Platform

Tech Solutions Ltd. experiences a denial of service attack that disrupts its e-commerce platform, resulting in significant loss of online sales. The Policyholder activates its incident response plan and collaborates with internet service providers to mitigate the attack. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. provides Business Interruption coverage to compensate for lost income and additional expenses incurred during the recovery process
. The Policyholder conducts a post-incident analysis to strengthen its defenses against future denial of service attacks.
9.4 Hypothetical Scenario: Insider Threat Leading to Data Theft

An employee of Tech Solutions Ltd. uses privileged access to steal sensitive intellectual property and sell it to a competitor. The Policyholder detects the unauthorized data transfer through its monitoring systems and takes immediate action to terminate the employee’s access and initiate legal proceedings. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. covers the costs of forensic investigation and legal representation under the Network Security Liability and Technology Errors and Omissions Liability coverages
. The Policyholder also enhances its access control measures and employee training programs to mitigate the risk of future insider threats.
9.5 Hypothetical Scenario: Social Engineering Fraud Targeting Finance Department

Tech Solutions Ltd. falls victim to a social engineering attack where cybercriminals impersonate a senior executive and instruct the finance department to transfer funds to an offshore account. The Policyholder realizes the fraud after the transfer is completed and reports the incident to SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd

. Ltd. The Social Engineering Fraud Endorsement provides coverage for the financial loss, and the Policyholder implements additional verification procedures to prevent similar incidents in the future.
10. Legal Implications and Compliance
10.1 Data Protection and Privacy Laws:

The Policyholder must comply with applicable data protection and privacy laws, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Personal Data Protection Bill (PDPB) in India. Compliance includes obtaining consent for data processing, implementing data subject rights, and reporting data breaches to relevant authorities within statutory timeframes. Non-compliance may result in regulatory fines and penalties, which are partially covered under the policy.

10.2 Cybersecurity Regulations:
Tech Solutions Ltd. is required to adhere to industry-specific cybersecurity regulations, such as those applicable to financial services, healthcare, or critical infrastructure sectors. Compliance involves implementing baseline security controls, conducting regular risk assessments, and reporting significant Cyber Incidents to regulatory bodies. The Policyholder should maintain documentation of compliance efforts and be prepared for regulatory audits.
10.3 Contractual Obligations:

The Policyholder must fulfill its contractual obligations related to cybersecurity and data protection, as specified in agreements with customers, partners, and service providers. This includes adhering to service level agreements, implementing specified security measures, and reporting Cyber Incidents that may impact contractual relationships. Failure to comply with contractual obligations may result in legal disputes, which are covered under Technology Errors and Omissions Liability.

10.4 Intellectual Property Rights:
Tech Solutions Ltd. must respect intellectual property rights and avoid unauthorized use of copyrighted materials, trademarks, or trade secrets. The Policyholder should conduct due diligence to ensure compliance with intellectual property laws and seek legal advice when necessary. While the policy excludes coverage for patent infringement, it provides Media Liability coverage for claims related to defamation, copyright infringement, and invasion of privacy.

10.5 Cross-Border Data Transfers:
The Policyholder must comply with legal requirements for cross-border data transfers, including obtaining necessary approvals and implementing data transfer agreements. Compliance with international data protection standards is essential to avoid legal challenges and ensure the protection of personal data. The Policyholder should seek guidance from legal experts to navigate complex data transfer regulations and mitigate associated risks.
10.6 Insurance Regulations and Disclosure Requirements:

SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. operates in compliance with applicable insurance regulations and disclosure requirements. The Policyholder must provide accurate and complete information during the underwriting process and promptly report any changes in risk exposure. Failure to disclose material information may result in denial of coverage or cancellation of the policy. SecureNet Insurance Pvt. Ltd. is committed to transparency and ethical conduct in all insurance transactions.
